notes.pr.303: The stone that draws up the statue is called achates (agate), though what is described is a magnet's pull. 'The Ptolemaid's palace' (Ptolomaidos aulae) is uncertain: the queen's palace, or the palace at Ptolemais.

nodes.text: not Philo of Athens, not he who, praised by his enemy,
drew out the famous struggles of the Syracusan war;
perhaps, too, the famed labours of men and of works
the Hebdomad, celebrated in the tenth volume of Marcus,
held here; here flourished the arts of famous Menecrates,
and the hand admired at Ephesus, or, on Minerva's citadel,
Ictinus, whose owl, smeared over with magic dye,
lures birds of every kind and kills them by its gaze.
Here perhaps was the founder of the Ptolemaid's palace,
Dinochares, for whom the square pyramid, in a cone toward its apex,
rises, and itself consumes its own shadows;
who once, commanded because of the bond of an incestuous love,
hung Arsinoe in the air of the Pharian temple.
For the agate in the vault of the roof breathes out its force
and draws the girl, breathed upon, by her iron-bound hair.
These, then, or men like these, it is fair to believe
set up the façades of houses in the lands of the Belgae,
